nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What does the preference for high group imply regarding social relations?
nodes.answer: A preference for high group implies a tendency towards collective decisions in organizing interactions among people.
nodes.paragraph: Each worldview represents a coherent package of pat- terns of social relations and cultural biases. Cultural biases are shared fundamental values (equality, freedom, order, and good/bad luck) and beliefs (underlying problem definitions, positions, strategies, and preferred policy instruments) about human and physical nature related to the four types of social relations (Newman et al., 2018; Oli & Swedlow, 2022; Sotirov & Winkel, 2016). Social relations refer to two dimensions: a preference for low or high external rules on human behavior called grid (thus more or less individual free- dom or constraints) and a preference for low or high group , referring to people S prefer - ence of how to organize their interactions with people (ranging from individual choices to collective decisions). The worldviews with their cultural biases and corresponding social relations and their reciprocal reinforcement are hence conceptualized through a grid-group typology (Thompson et al., 1990; see also Sotirov & Winkel, 2016, Swedlow, 2012). The four worldviews are summarized in Fig. 1. Each quadrant along the two axes of high/low group and grid represents one worldview.

nodes.question: What are the two dimensions referred to in social relations?
nodes.answer: The two dimensions are a preference for low or high external rules on human behavior (grid) and a preference for low or high group interactions.

nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What concept does the text elaborate on using a biosemiotics reading of Luhmann's social theory?
nodes.answer: The text elaborates on the concept of societal identity.
nodes.paragraph: The text is organized as follows. We first provide theoretical support for the original interpretation of the bioeconomy that it is incompatible with the idea of green growth ( Understanding the functioning of living systems ). We then show, in biophysical terms, that the evolutionary path of human society has moved away rather than toward a bioeconomy ( Rupture of the equilibrium between society and environment: the metabolic rift ). Following, we examine the factors and circumstances that have led many to believe that the idea of nature as a mentor endorses the conviction that technologies and business models can fix our sustainability problems. To this purpose, we first elaborate the concept of societal identity, using a biosemiotics reading of the social theory of Luhmann ( The changing societal identity ) and then analyze the sociotechnical imaginaries sustaining the current social identity ( Implausible sociotechnical imaginaries? ). Lastly, we elaborate on the information disorder that has resulted from the systemic use of implausible sociotechnical imaginaries, in particular the current interpretation of the bioeconomy concept in the sustainability political discourse ( Information disorder ). The final section provides the conclusion.
